ON FLUIDITY

We have distinguished between the two previous cases because, in those, we supposed that certain extraneous corpuscles were introduced into the body, which contributed to its firmness and (even if perhaps only in a small quantity) entered into its constitution. In this instance, however, we suppose that those particles do not materially combine to constitute the body upon which they operate; rather, they merely agitate and move the constituent particles of the body in various ways, perhaps breaking some, bending and entangling others, and, in a word, changing the texture so that those parts which were previously either moving separately or adhering less strictly are now reduced into a tighter space or a more entangled texture, and by this method are more firmly connected to one another. That the mere arrangement of the parts of a body in relation to one another, with no added extrinsic material, can contribute greatly to stability, may be seen both in certain examples mentioned previously and in wicker rods. When these are loose and lying in a pile, they can easily be separated from one another, but when woven into a basket, they adhere so firmly that, if one is lifted, all the rest are lifted with it.
